The Spanish Armada. In fifteen eighty-eight, King Philip II of Spain sent a massive naval invasion fleet against Elizabeth I's England, intended to conquer the island and overthrow the Protestant queen. Though assembled with superior numbers and advanced galleons, the Spanish fleet was defeated by English tactics, superior seamanship, and fortunate storms, marking a turning point in naval power and securing England's independence from Spanish intervention.

Philip II, Catholicism's champion, saw Protestant England as a heretical threat and a base for pirates. Decades of English privateers had attacked Spanish treasure fleets, and England had supported Spanish rebels in the Netherlands, all motivating the invasion. The Spanish Armada consisted of one hundred thirty ships carrying roughly thirty thousand men. It was assembled with meticulous planning and considerable expense, representing the greatest naval power then afloat and the most advanced warship designs of the era.

English tactics proved decisive. Rather than attempting boarding actions, which was the Spanish specialty, English captains maintained distance and used superior gunfire and maneuverability. English cannon fire damaged Spanish ships more effectively than Spanish attempts to return fire. A combination of English naval tactics, Spanish organizational problems including the death of the original commander before departure, and fortunate weather including an Atlantic storm that scattered the Spanish fleet all contributed to the Armada's defeat.

After two weeks of skirmishes, the Armada withdrew northward and attempted to return to Spain by sailing around Scotland and Ireland. Rough seas, inadequate supplies, and lack of shelter destroyed many ships. Roughly fifty percent of the fleet was lost. The victory established England as a genuine naval power, secured Elizabeth's reign against foreign conquest, and marked the beginning of English naval supremacy that would persist for three centuries. It became a cultural touchstone of English identity and Protestant victory.
